prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which many atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength, and their development to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: I keep B001 alone, with Katori and Ye, as my final position. Having read all eight first-round statements, the case is the same one I made in round 1, and it has not been weakened by anything said. It is a quantitative result that is understood from atomic theory down to each systematic shift, reproduced by several independent laboratories that compare clocks across sites, and checkable by nature: millimetre-to-centimetre gravitational redshift, bounds on varying constants and on dark-matter couplings. The concept is distinct: trapping many neutral atoms where the light shift cancels, which gave the statistical power and the control over collisions and blackbody shifts that brought the uncertainty to 10^-18. The citation should name that lattice concept and its realisation, not clocks or precision in general, so that it does not claim ground already covered in 2005 and 2012. Attribution is cleaner than for any condensed-matter candidate, where a three-name cap forces cuts I cannot defend. I also checked, as I said I would, that I would hold this position if the support counts were hidden, and I would: the objections raised against B001 are about framing and priority detail, not about the physics being wrong or unconfirmed.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, which all eight of us raised, is that this reads as a refinement of the frequency-comb prize (2005) and the ion-clock and single-quantum-system prize (2012). I think the many-atom magic-wavelength scheme answers it, but I recognise that nobody has settled it, and a committee member could reasonably weigh it differently. Second, a two-name credit leaves out groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley, Campbell, and the Paris, NIST and PTB teams) that made decisive contributions; no member has verified the priority record and I cannot, from my own field, do so either. Third, I remain wary that I moved from my own first choice, B010, partly under the pull of consensus; the fact that four colleagues also moved does not itself make the move right. I have weighed that and still land here on the merits, but it is a real risk of how this discussion has gone. Finally, the SI second has not been redefined, which is a timing point, not a physical one.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the pending redefinition of the SI second should not delay the prize, since it is a metrological decision following from the physics, and that the lattice clock is a new capability, not a polish.
responses.response: I agree and I have moved on this. In round 1 I listed the redefinition as a possible reason to wait; I now think waiting would tie a physics prize to an administrative milestone. What persuades me is your point that the reduction by about two orders of magnitude over the best ion clocks opened applications the earlier clocks could not reach. I would want the citation to say so through the lattice concept, and not through the second.

responses.point: Danielsson, as Secretary, would want external expert reports to confirm the priority record of the magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice clock and the 10^-18 result, and counts the exclusion of other groups as a risk.
responses.response: I support that request, because it is the one open factual question that could change my vote. I cannot judge the sequence from my own field, and the chair's question 2 asks the same. If an external reviewer finds that a third group has a priority claim equal to Katori's or Ye's, I would reconsider the two-name credit. Short of that, I think Katori's proposal and first realisation, and Ye's record performance and many-body clock physics, are the two steps that are hardest to substitute, so I keep the pair.

responses.point: Lindroth says the lattice clock opened a genuinely different many-atom regime, and also doubts B042 because choosing three of five names is arbitrary and the payoff beyond classical computation is not yet shown.
responses.response: I agree on both. You are closest to the atomic physics and your reading, that the lattice clock is a different regime from the comb and from single ions, is what carries my answer to the overlap question. On B042 I share your doubts, and I would not add it as a second part: the theory and experiment split under five names cannot be cut to three without removing a founder, and the quantum-simulation payoff is still ahead. That is why I do not propose a two-part prize.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B006 and B004 as alternatives and notes that credit in topological insulators is split between Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Fu-Kane-Mele and Hasan.
responses.response: Your point about the split credit is the main reason I do not push B010 in the preferred configuration, even though I think it is a real new class of matter and that the 2016 prize covered topological phases and quantum Hall-type invariants, not time-reversal-invariant materials. Between B010 and B004 I find the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp set the better defended, since the HgTe measurement confirmed a quantitative prediction. But I still do not see a three-name set that represents the history, so I keep it as an alternative. On B006, I share your own doubt about first-order melting and the closeness to 2016.

responses.point: Johansson moved circuit QED (B003) from first place to an alternative because of proximity to the 2025 prize, and recuses himself from B003, while treating B001 as a clean measurement that nature can check.
responses.response: I agree that B003 is a poor fit for this year, and I respect that you stated your connection plainly. A second circuit prize directly after the 2025 one on macroscopic quantum tunnelling would look repetitive, and the four-name allocation between Girvin and Blais is not resolved. I would still not rule it out in a later year. I do not think the committee needs to rule on it now, since nobody proposes it as a part.

responses.point: Olsson now places B001 first on the grounds that the lattice clock is an original invention reproduced in many laboratories, and she keeps B017 and B015 as open questions, asking whether the 1995 discovery or the MgO step would be honoured for B015.
responses.response: Your test, original idea plus independent verification, is the one I apply to B001. I agree that B015 has an unsettled credit question: Miyazaki and Moodera in 1995, the MgO step with Parkin, Yuasa and Djayaprawira, the Butler and Mathon band-structure theory, and Julliere's 1975 precursor cannot all be fitted into three names. On B017 I keep it as an alternative, and I accept that its pairing mechanism is open.

uncertainties: Whether an external or specialist check of the priority record (magic-wavelength proposal, first strontium lattice clock, 10^-18 result) would support a two-name credit.
Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I judge that it is, but I cannot show that the objection is settled.
How credit would be divided among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan and others if B010 were revisited, and whether the pairing mechanism in B017 will be clarified soon.
Whether my move from B010 to B001 is driven partly by wish for consensus, which I have tried to test but cannot fully rule out.
statement.conflict_note: No change. I have no known collaboration with Katori, Ye or any other credited person on the shortlist. I disclose only general proximity to the condensed-matter candidates (B010, B017) through my first-principles electronic-structure group, and I note that Johansson has recused himself on B003 and that I have no tie to that candidate.
